The Northern leatherside chub Lepidomeda copei attains a maximum recorded total length of 15 cm [Li = 15 cm], a size that places it among the smaller cyprinids endemic to the Bonneville Basin of the western United States. Field surveys indicate that the onset of sexual maturation occurs at a body length of 5.3 cm [Lp = 5.3 cm], a threshold that corresponds closely with the size at which first spawning activity has been documented. At this stage, individuals have reached a wet body weight of 1.47 g [Wwp = 1.47 g], reflecting the modest somatic investment required to initiate reproductive function in this species. Newly emerged yolk-sac larvae, hatching from eggs with a mean diameter of approximately one millimeter, possess a remarkably small birth weight of 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], highlighting the extreme altricial condition of the offspring at the moment of chorion rupture. This initial mass is orders of magnitude below the eventual asymptotic body weight, which, based on length-weight regressions from mature adults, reaches 35.4 grams [Wwi = 35.4 grams] in fully grown individuals.

Laboratory rearing experiments conducted at a constant water temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C] have provided valuable insights into the reproductive biology of Lepidomeda copei. Under these conditions, females typically deposit between 1 and 3 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 1 and 3 eggs per spawning event], and they are capable of producing approximately 1.5 such clutches each year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 such clutches each year]. This relatively low annual fecundity is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring survival in the cold, stable headwater streams this minnow inhabits. The sustained reproductive output at this temperature is notable, as it suggests that 6 °C [T = 6 °C] lies well within the species’ thermal optimum for gametogenesis and spawning behavior. Comparable data from related Western cyprinids suggest that reproductive rates at warmer temperatures may be somewhat higher, but L. copei appears adapted to a narrow thermal regime that limits metabolic scope and, consequently, the frequency of reproductive bouts.

The egg size of Lepidomeda copei, measured at roughly one millimeter in diameter, dictates the initial wet mass of the developing embryo prior to eclosion. Fertilized ova are demersal and slightly adhesive, a trait that aids in maintaining position within the gravel interstices of the species’ preferred spawning riffles. The yolk-laden egg contains sufficient endogenous nutrition to support the endotrophic larva through the first several days post-hatching, during which the yolk-sac larva remains largely immobile within the substrate. The calculated birth weight of 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams] for newly emerged prolarvae aligns closely with predictions based on egg geometry, confirming that early developmental stages are heavily dependent on yolk reserves. Once the yolk absorption is complete and the mouth opens, the transition to exogenous feeding marks a critical period of high mortality, as the small size of the larvae makes them vulnerable to starvation and predation. Larval metamorphosis proceeds gradually over several weeks, culminating in the recruitment of post-metamorphic juveniles to the benthic habitat.

Longevity records for the Northern leatherside chub, derived from mark-recapture studies in thermally stable spring-fed systems, indicate that the species can live for as long as 8 years [am = 8 years] under favorable conditions at 6 °C [T = 6 °C]. This extended lifespan is somewhat unusual for a fish of its body size and is likely a consequence of its evolution in cold, unproductive environments where metabolic rates are chronically depressed. The corresponding generation time, estimated from the age of mature individuals in wild populations, is considerably shorter than the maximum lifespan, reflecting the iteroparous reproductive strategy that allows multiple spawning events across several seasons. In warmer, more variable streams outside its core habitat, observed lifespans tend to be shorter, suggesting that temperature exerts a strong influence on somatic maintenance and senescence rates. The 8-year maximum (8 years) [am = 8 years] was recorded in a population occupying a stable headwater reach of the Thomas Fork, where annual temperature variation is minimal at a temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C].

Adult body condition in Lepidomeda copei shows a pronounced allometric relationship between length and weight, with mature individuals at the ultimate length of 15 cm [Li = 15 cm] attaining a maximum wet body mass of 35.4 grams [Wwi = 35.4 grams]. This length-weight relationship, derived from a large sample of sexually mature adults collected across multiple drainages, provides a reliable basis for estimating condition factors and comparing energetic status among populations. Individuals at the point of sexual maturation, measuring 5.3 cm [Lp = 5.3 cm] in total length, exhibit a corresponding body mass of 1.47 grams [Wwp = 1.47 grams], indicating a substantial increase in mass per unit length as the fish grows toward its asymptotic size. The transition from the pubertal weight of roughly 1.47 g to the ultimate adult weight of over 35 grams [Wwi = over 35 grams] spans a remarkable 24-fold increase, underscoring the prolonged growth trajectory characteristic of this cold-water specialist.
